title: Session-proxy SDK patterns for chunked JSON emissions and callback wiring (TS/Py/Go)
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: App developers integrate LLM features that emit JSON-like semantic objects as they stream (e.g., incremental parse trees, partial tool outputs). Current SDK surfaces in TS/Py/Go don't provide a minimal, consistent abstraction to: 1) reassemble framed/chunked JSON events reliably across transports, 2) propagate tool/function call intents as structured callback events, and 3) expose a single ergonomic session object for partial results + finalization.

Goal: Implement a lightweight "session-proxy" layer inside each SDK that normalizes server streaming envelopes into language-native primitives (event stream iterator/callbacks + final resolved object). Provide language-consistent examples showing: progressive partial JSON emission, out-of-band tool-call events, graceful fallback to non-streaming responses, and a compatibility shim for older SDK surfaces.

Why different from previous tickets: many prior tickets focused on framing or typed adapters; this one formalizes a small runtime session object pattern that SDK users can adopt with minimal changes and ties together partial JSON assembly + tool callback wiring in one UX. The implementation emphasizes discoverability and few surface APIs rather than exposing low-level framing primitives.
acceptance_criteria: TS/Py/Go SDKs expose a SessionProxy (or equivalent) with: on_event(callback), on_tool(callback), next_chunk() iterator/async-iterator, and finalize() that returns the assembled JSON object as the final result.

Framing: SDK handles chunk boundaries, escaped newlines, and incremental partial-object patches (diff-patch or complete fragments) such that downstream consumers see valid intermediate objects where possible.
Tool calls: Server-emitted tool-call events are surfaced as structured objects with metadata (tool_id, args, request_id) and the SDK can mark tool results as injected back into the session stream.
Backward compatibility: Existing high-level generate()/chat() call sites continue to work; streaming opt-in uses new session APIs without breaking non-streaming code.
End-to-end tests for each language covering: single-object stream, multi-object stream, tool-call mid-stream and tool result injection, and fallback to non-streaming response.
design_notes:
High-level architecture: introduce SessionProxy abstraction inside SDK core. On HTTP/HTTP2 (hosted) or Websocket long-polling (private/dedicated), the proxy normalizes raw frames into normalized 'Envelope' events: {type: 'partial', payload: string|jsonFragment, seq: int, request_id: uuid} and {type: 'tool_call', tool_id, args, request_id}. The SDK then assembles payloads by either concatenating fragments or applying small merge heuristics (when server emits 'patch' vs 'flush' flags). The proxy exposes two consumption patterns: 1) event-driven callbacks (on_event, on_tool), 2) iterator-based consumption (async iterator in TS/Py, channel in Go). For tool call round-trips the proxy will: pause token emission to the app, surface tool call, accept tool result (via session.inject_tool_result(...)), then continue stream.

Envelope schema decisions: prefer text-first payloads (string fragments) to avoid double-JSON-encoding. Provide a compact 'event_metadata' header for ordering and checksum. Server will tag 'final' and 'close' events.

Error handling: out-of-order fragments will be buffered up to a reasonable window (configurable, default 10s/50 fragments). If assembly fails, SDK will emit a 'malformed_fragment' diagnostic event and fall back to raw text stream (no crash).

Telemetry: SDK should emit instrumentation hooks (counters for fragments, tool-calls, reassembly errors) that Console can surface later.

Backward compat shim: an opt-in compatibility flag config.session_proxy: 'on'|'off' (default on) so older customers can disable if they built their own framing logic.
implementation_plan: Define minimal cross-language SessionProxy interface and example signatures in ADR (doc link below)
Implement core reassembly engine in TypeScript; wire into node/browser HTTP SSE and websocket clients
Port core reassembly logic to Python (sync/async) using same tests
Implement Go version using channels and context cancellation ergonomics
Add tool-call wiring (server -> SDK event -> app callback -> SDK.inject_tool_result)
Add feature flag config and backward compat shim
Write unit tests, integration tests with a local mock server that emits framed events
Add docs + quickstart examples for all three languages
Ship beta behind SDK opt-in and run dogfooding with internal Console features
progress_updates: 2026-03-05: Ticket created and initial ADR drafted. Linked design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/c/SESSION-PROXY-ADR
2026-03-07: PoC reassembly engine implemented in TS (repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/842). Initial tests for concatenated fragments pass.
2026-03-10: Design review with Platform and Runtime teams — decided on text-first fragments and 10s buffer window. Note: runtime will add 'patch' flag in a follow-up (ENG-179999).
2026-03-12: Python async iterator API sketched; blocker found in existing SSE client behavior when applying backpressure (workaround planned)
2026-03-13: Go channel API prototype completed and demoed to SDK working group. Preparing PRs for review. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/859
qa_plan: Unit tests for reassembly logic with randomized fragmentation patterns
Integration test using mock server to simulate tool-call mid-stream and injected result
Load test: measure reassembly latency and memory under 1000 concurrent sessions
Cross-language smoke tests: run TS/Py/Go examples in CI matrix
Manual dogfood: enable in internal Console for 24 hours and capture errors/usage
notes: Design trade-offs: we prioritize ergonomics and small surface area over exposing every low-level envelope field. Long-term we may expose a lower-level framed API for advanced users, but this ticket purposely avoids that complexity. Keep the session proxy implementation small (< 300 lines per language core).
